items.title: A Wild Himalayan Spice Is Helping 200 Families Protect 100 Sq Km of Forest
items.blurb: On autumn mornings in Arunachal Pradesh's West Kameng district , families head into the forest carrying woven bamboo baskets. They are not looking for timber or firewood. Instead, they are searching for a thorny shrub that has quietly shaped local food, medicine and trade for generations. Known locally as Khagi, Erma, Shyein or Yarma , depending on the tribe and region, Zanthoxylum is a wild Himalayan spice whose tiny fruits release a sharp citrus aroma followed by a tingling numbness on the tongue. Long before it found buyers beyond the mountains, it flavoured meat curries, chutneys and millet dishes in tribal homes. Its bark, fruits and seeds were also used in indigenous healing traditions. Khagi tastes citrusy, sharp, and peppery. It has a strong aroma resembling lemon or grapefruit. Photograph: (WWF-India) Today, that same spice is helping protect more than 100 sq km of community-owned forests. The transformation did not happen overnight. Over the past few years, WWF India has been working with Indigenous communities and traditional village institutions to strengthen Community Conserved Areas (CCAs) across Arunachal Pradesh. Community Conserved Areas are natural ecosystems such as forests, wetlands and grasslands that are voluntarily protected and managed by Indigenous and local communities. Their stewardship helps conserve habitats, wildlife and biodiversity while ensuring forests continue to support local livelihoods. One of the strongest examples has emerged in the Mandala Phudung Khellong Community Conserved Area (CCA) in West Kameng district. Here, villagers have linked the future of their forests with the future of Khagi. Community Conserved Areas are natural ecosystems such as forests, wetlands and grasslands that are voluntarily protected and managed by Indigenous and local communities. Photograph: (WWF-India) By creating a community-led system to sustainably harvest, aggregate and market the spice, they have turned a native forest species into a source of income that rewards conservation rather than extraction. Today, every kilogram of Khagi sold contributes towards forest patrols, biodiversity monitoring and community welfare, giving people a direct economic reason to keep thousands of hectares of forest standing. A forest owned by its people Arunachal Pradesh is unlike most states in India when it comes to forests. Nearly 80% of its geographical area is under forest cover, while more than 60% of these forests are classified as Unclassed State Forests, remaining under the de facto custodianship of Indigenous communities and traditional institutions. The state is also one of India's richest biodiversity landscapes. It is home to two global biodiversity hotspots, over a quarter of India's plant species, the country's highest mammalian diversity and more than 1,600 high-altitude lakes. That community ownership makes local decisions especially important. #DidYouKnow Zanthoxylum, locally known as Khagei or Zabrang, is an essential condiment in the Monpa area of Western Arunachal Pradesh. It is part of the local diet and used as chutney and pickle. Read more about the partnership here: https://t.co/g8UGhkvUMM pic.twitter.com/U19AtBDUKs — WWF-India (@WWFINDIA) March 21, 2020 Across Arunachal Pradesh, many villages have voluntarily established Community Conserved Areas, where Indigenous communities decide how forests should be used, which activities should be restricted and how benefits should be shared. Unlike government-declared protected areas, these forests are governed through community consensus. However, as communities gradually shift from subsistence livelihoods to cash-based economies, many traditional governance systems have weakened. Expanding roads and infrastructure have also fragmented fragile mountain habitats. The CCA model offers a different path — one where economic opportunities strengthen conservation instead of replacing it. The spice that was already there Khagi did not arrive with a conservation project. The shrub has always grown naturally across abandoned agricultural fields and adjoining forests around Mandala. For generations, families harvested enough for their kitchens and sold the surplus in nearby markets. Its history stretches back even further. Communities in Kalaktang and Dirang once supplied the aromatic spice as tribute to the Tsona Dzong and Tawang Monastery . From there, it travelled across mountain passes such as Bumla into Tibet, becoming part of long-standing Himalayan trade routes . Despite its cultural and commercial importance, however, the trade remained fragmented. Families harvested individually, while traders from Tezpur, Guwahati and elsewhere purchased produce directly from villages, often offering different prices. Only the outer husk had commercial demand. The seeds were usually discarded because there was no market for them. The result was limited bargaining power, little value addition and no collective investment in the forests where the spice naturally grew. Turning harvest into conservation Things began to change in 2019. Supported by WWF India under the Community Conserved Area framework, villagers organised themselves to collectively harvest, aggregate and market Khagi. The initiative also established direct market linkages with companies such as Dabur India, allowing communities to sell both the husk and the seeds instead of treating part of the harvest as waste. The change went far beyond marketing. Every August, as the harvesting season begins, families head into the forests to handpick ripe Khagi from shrubs growing across abandoned farmlands and adjoining forest patches. Back home, the fruits are spread out under the sun to dry for several days before being sorted and sold. Not every harvest reaches the market. "Our partnership with companies has made a significant difference by bringing a reliable market for Khagi right to our doorstep," says Phurpu, a member of the Mandala Phudung Khellong CCA Management Committee. Photograph: (WWF-India) Many families keep aside a portion for their own kitchens, where Khagi has long been a staple ingredient. It is ground into chutneys with tomatoes, local onions, fermented soybean, chhurpi and chillies, adding its signature citrusy heat to rice, smoked meat and seasonal vegetables. Today, that familiar seasonal ritual also contributes to protecting the forests that have sustained these communities for generations. During the last two harvesting seasons, between 2024 and 2026, communities sold more than 10 metric tonnes of Zanthoxylum, benefiting over 200 households and generating a turnover of around Rs 39 lakh. Around Rs 6 lakh was contributed to the Community Conserved Area Management Fund. It is a cycle the community designed for itself. "Our partnership with companies has made a significant difference by bringing a reliable market for Khagi right to our doorstep," says Phurpu, a member of the Mandala Phudung Khellong CCA Management Committee. "Earlier, traders from Assam and other parts of the state offered different prices. Now, community members can sell their harvest within the village at a fair and uniform price through one transparent transaction." The benefits, however, differ from one household to another. Families in Mandala Phudung Khellong do not depend on Khagi alone. Most also cultivate kiwi, tomatoes, cabbage, beans and other seasonal crops, making the spice one part of a broader livelihood. According to community members who spoke to The Better India , households that primarily depend on farming earn around Rs 5,000 to Rs 10,000 from Khagi during a harvesting season, while their annual farm income generally ranges between Rs 20,000 and Rs 30,000, depending on the scale of cultivation. "For many years, every family sold Khagi on its own, and we never knew what price others were getting or where the produce finally went," says Pem Choijang, the Gaonburah (traditional village headman) of Mandala Phudung village Photograph: (WWF-India) For families harvesting larger quantities, the returns are higher. The additional income helps meet household expenses and purchase seeds and farm inputs for the next season. Rather than replacing agriculture, Khagi has become an important supplementary source of income — one that also gives communities a direct stake in keeping their forests healthy. Rules that came from the village Income alone cannot conserve forests. Alongside the new value chain, the community developed a management plan to protect biodiversity. Working with the traditional Mangma institution and Panchayati Raj Institutions, the CCA Management Committee established rules restricting hunting, regulating resource use and prohibiting commercial extraction unless sustainable management practices had been approved. Funds generated through Khagi marketing, together with technical and financial support from WWF India and the Forest Department, now support regular forest patrols and biodiversity monitoring. For village elders, transparency has been just as important as income. "For many years, every family sold Khagi on its own, and we never knew what price others were getting or where the produce finally went," says Pem Choijang, the Gaonburah (traditional village headman) of Mandala Phudung village. "Different traders offered different prices, so there was little transparency and very little bargaining power. I have seen how things have changed over the years. "We can now collectively market Khagi at a uniform price through a transparent process agreed upon by the Mangma and the CCA Management Committee. "The income doesn't stop with individual households. It also supports forest protection, biodiversity monitoring and village welfare. That has changed the way people look at our forests. They are no longer just places where we collect resources — they are something we all share the responsibility to protect." The system has also enabled communities to engage more actively in discussions around road alignments that minimise impacts on forests and wildlife habitats. A forest worth keeping intact The Mandala Phudung Khellong Community Conserved Area borders Bhutan's Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary, creating an important transboundary conservation landscape. Its forests provide habitat and movement corridors for species including the clouded leopard, Asian golden cat, marbled cat, Himalayan black bear, red panda, large Indian civet, Arunachal macaque, capped langur, goral and Himalayan serow. Pheasants have also been recorded within the landscape. The forests are equally important for people. Medicinal and economically valuable plants such as Swertia chirayita, Illicium griffithii, Rubia cordifolia, Paris polyphylla and Zanthoxylum continue to support traditional healthcare systems and local livelihoods. We work to explore the potential of non-timber forest products (NTFPs) collected from the forests of Mandala Phudung Khellong CCA (MPKCCA) and establish market linkages. Six main NTFPs were identified as species & harvested for commercial purposes. pic.twitter.com/6CSYCwZKvJ — WWF-India (@WWFINDIA) March 21, 2020 While formal impact studies are still underway, communities report more frequent sightings of wildlife, including red pandas, alongside visible forest recovery. Just as important, conservation-linked livelihoods have strengthened local stewardship. Income from sustainable harvesting is now reinvested into patrolling, biodiversity monitoring and implementing community rules. Instead of seeing forests only as land to be converted, communities increasingly see intact ecosystems as assets that continue generating livelihoods year after year. A different conservation story For decades, conservation has often been framed as a choice between protecting forests and supporting local livelihoods. Mandala Phudung Khellong tells a completely different story. The community did not introduce an exotic crop or replace forests with plantations. Instead, it built an economy around a species that already belonged to the landscape and had long been part of local culture. That decision transformed Khagi from a household spice into a reason to keep forests standing. This story is part of a content series by The Better India and WWF-India. items.title: This Kerala Mother's 16-Year Fight for Her Differently-Abled Daughter Became a Lifeline for 200 Other Mothers
items.blurb: On 25 March 2010, in a hospital in Kerala’s Thiruvananthapuram, Sheeja gave birth to her daughter, Sandra. Within hours, doctors delivered a diagnosis that would reshape the next sixteen years of her life. Sandra had microcephaly, a rare condition in which the brain does not develop sufficiently. Many children born with it do not survive. Sandra did. However, survival, Sheeja would learn, was only the beginning . What followed were years that blurred into one another, filled with hospital corridors, ICU rooms, ventilators, and the constant cycle of seizures that sometimes struck twenty times a day. Medication was non-negotiable, expensive, and tireless. So was care. Somewhere within that cycle of urgency, Sheeja says she stopped recognising the life she had once imagined. “It is a birth defect. We could not do anything, and we accepted it as fate. But it broke me,” she says simply, as if naming something that had taken years to understand. At home, the strain intensified at first and then all at once. As medical bills mounted and caregiving became a full-time responsibility, her marriage collapsed. Her husband eventually left. But Sandra stayed, and so did the caregiving. What Sheeja did not yet have words for was what she was beginning to see everywhere around her. There were other mothers, each carrying similar stories and each learning to disappear into them. Early life before the diagnosis Before Sandra’s birth, Sheeja’s life had followed a more ordinary pace. She studied in Thiruvananthapuram , attended Manchadi Government LP School and later St Xavier’s School in Peyad. She was drawn more to sports and social work than textbooks, and married during her degree course with the understanding that she would continue studying afterwards. Sandra changed that trajectory completely. ⁠In India, women shoulder nearly three times more unpaid care work than men, making mothers of children with disabilities especially vulnerable to financial hardship after leaving paid jobs. The hospital became a second home. Days were framed in admissions and emergencies rather than hours or months. Over time, Sheeja completed her degree and teacher training, but formal employment remained out of reach. She turned instead to tailoring and other work from home, supported at defining moments by her parents, Babu and Usha, who helped care for Sandra whenever they could. That support, however, was not something she could assume others had. “In government hospital wards, I began noticing a pattern that unsettled me more with each visit. Mothers were sitting alone beside children with disabilities. Some spoke of husbands who stopped coming after the diagnosis. Others had already been abandoned entirely,” she tells The Better India. It was in these waiting rooms that Sheeja first met Vidya. Slow disappearance of identity Vidya had once been a mathematics teacher at a private school in Kerala’s Attingal. Her son, Aadi, is now nine years old and lives with cerebral palsy. The diagnosis did not just alter her family’s routine. It gradually ended her career. “I kept thinking I would go back after a year,” she says. “Then the year became three, and then it became never.” Work was replaced by caregiving . Her identity gradually narrowed to medical charts, therapy sessions, and hospital visits. When she eventually met Sheeja at a hospital, what struck her most was not sympathy, but recognition. For many caregivers, the biggest cost of disability is not medical treatment alone but the income lost when one parent is forced to become a full-time caregiver. “People used to ask me what I did,” Vidya says. “Now they only ask what is wrong with my son. I became his condition instead of staying myself.” It was a feeling Sheeja was beginning to recognise in herself as well. Hospital corridors and the breaking point The idea that would eventually become ‘Snehasandram Charitable Trust’ did not arrive as a plan. It accumulated, incident by incident, over years spent in hospitals. There were moments Sheeja still returns to unwillingly . A couple she knew, overwhelmed by the prospect of lifelong care, attempted suicide along with their disabled child. The parents did not survive. The child did. Today, the child is being raised by the grandmother. Another time, a mother she had met briefly handed her disabled child to Sheeja in a hospital corridor, said she would return shortly, and walked away. She went to the fifth floor and did not come back down. “These are not isolated stories,” Sheeja says. “They are the ones you hear about. Most are never spoken of.” What stayed with her most was grief and the absence of anyone consistently standing beside these mothers. ⁠In Kerala, one family's donated stack of old newspapers can help fund medicines, wheelchairs or emergency supplies for another family caring for a child with disabilities. That absence became the foundation of Snehasandram. Building trust for mothers alone When she registered the Snehasandram Charitable Trust in August 2021, she made a decision that defined everything that followed — though its roots trace back further, to the years Sheeja spent moving between hospital wards. Membership would be open only to mothers raising children with disabilities. She believed only they could genuinely understand one another without explanation. The trust began with something deceptively humble. It began with work. It started offering sewing machines, tailoring training, and livelihood support through activities such as goat and poultry rearing. The aim was not charity in the traditional sense, but stability. “We never wanted them to depend on us. We wanted them to stand on their own again,” Sheeja says. Among the first to experience this shift was Shailey. Shailey and the end of waiting Shailey, 35, spends most mornings stitching blouse pieces in a small shared workspace supported by the trust. Her daughter has Down syndrome, and for years her life was defined by waiting. She waited outside special schools, waited for therapy sessions to end, and waited for a moment that belonged to her alone. “I used to sit outside the school gate for four hours because there was nowhere else to go,” she says. “I could not leave her, and I could not work.” Homeschooling has become an important alternative for some children with complex medical needs, allowing learning to continue despite frequent hospital visits or unpredictable health conditions. The trust changed how she spent those hours. They became working hours. Slowly, she began earning enough to cover part of her daughter’s physiotherapy expenses. “Last month, I paid for my daughter’s physiotherapy myself, without asking my father,” she explains. Rini and the gradual form of abandonment As the community grew, its response to crises grew with it. Members stepped in to arrange medicines when families ran out, source wheelchairs when mobility became urgent, and deliver diapers, food supplies, and other emergency essentials whenever they could. They held the network together not through formal structures, but through a shared sense of urgency. It is within this growing web that Rini’s story sits. Her husband did not walk away overnight. He left gradually. First, by coming home late. Then, by taking a job in Kochi. Then, by sending money for a few months. Then by stopping contact altogether. “He just faded away over time, and somehow that hurt more than if he had left,” she says. Her son lives with autism, and like many women in the group, she came to Snehasandram after years of struggle rather than one dramatic collapse. What she found was a room full of women who already understood. A growing community and an unfinished dream Today, Snehasandram supports more than 200 mothers across Thiruvananthapuram and nearby regions, including families in the Kottoor tribal settlement. ⁠Down syndrome, cerebral palsy, autism and microcephaly may all require long-term care, but each condition affects development differently and demands highly individualised support. The trust operates from a humble office in Pappanamcode, but much of its work happens in homes, hospitals and informal support networks. One of its most unusual lifelines comes from donated newspapers and magazines, collected from households and sold as scrap, with the proceeds used for emergency support for mothers. Over time, individual donors and CSR funding have added to this ecosystem, though the need continues to outpace resources. A 20-cent land donation in Thiruvananthapuram has now opened the possibility of a rehabilitation centre where children with disabilities can live alongside caregivers, allowing mothers to work without having to choose between earning an income and providing care. The estimated cost, around Rs 40 lakh, remains out of reach for now, but the vision remains unchanged. Sheeja Sandra and what survival looks like Sheeja has since added her daughter’s name to her own. She is now Sheeja Sandra, a decision she describes as permanence rather than symbolism. Looking at what has grown from hospital corridors into a network of more than 200 mothers, she does not speak in the language of achievement. She speaks instead of shared survival. “We are mothers who have failed life’s test again and again,” she says. “But every time we manage to help one another stand, that is a small win.” ⁠Down syndrome, cerebral palsy, autism and microcephaly may all require long-term care, but each condition affects development differently and demands highly individualised support. Outside her office, life continues in its uneven tempo, with calls from hospitals, requests for diapers, and urgent needs that cannot wait for planning. Inside, what holds it together is simpler: mothers who once sat alone in hospital corridors no longer have to do so. "We are mothers who have failed life's tests again and again," she says. "But every time we manage to help one another stand, that is a small win." Outside her office, life continues in its uneven tempo, with calls from hospitals, requests for diapers, and urgent needs that cannot wait for planning. Sandra, now sixteen, is a homeschooler studying under the Snehasandram Trust. While her seizures present themselves on the regular, she says she has support from all sides. “I don’t feel alone in this journey and neither does my mother. There are other women to support us and that’s what matters,” she said. A typical day in Sandra’s life including classes, studies and lots of curiosity-driven research she conducts using books independently. “Books are non-judgmental and I find solace in them,” she explains. For Sheeja, Sandra remains her pillar of strength — a constant reminder of how far she has come, not only in building a life for herself, but in creating one for the many other families who once had nowhere to turn. “I can’t believe we have come so far, but it is very fulfilling,” she says, before rushing back to the administrative work that keeps the trust running. It is a small, ordinary detail, but it is also the whole story in miniature: the mother-daughter duo for whom a diagnosis once emptied a room of possibility are now, in their own ways, part of the reason that room stays full for many others. Inside, what holds it together is simpler: mothers who once sat alone in hospital corridors no longer have to do so — and neither, anymore, is Sheeja.

items.title: Retired Army Officer Uses Century-Old Maps To Bring 14 Dry Bengaluru Lakes Back to Life
items.blurb: What happens when rain can no longer find the path it has followed for centuries? In Bengaluru, it floods roads instead of filling lakes. Every monsoon , cars stall in waterlogged streets, homes flood, and the city slows after a few hours of heavy rain. Yet several lakes remain dry. For retired Army officer Captain Santosh Kumar, the contradiction demanded an answer. If the city received enough rain to flood entire neighbourhoods, why was that water failing to reach its lakes? The answer lay beneath roads, buildings and decades of urban expansion, inside Bengaluru’s forgotten network of Raja Kaluves. These ancient channels carried rainwater from one lake to another, protecting the city from floods while replenishing its water bodies. Using British-era maps from 1923, Captain Santosh began tracing the waterways Bengaluru had buried. Why Bengaluru’s rain stopped reaching its lakes Captain Santosh retired from the Army in 2008 and returned to Muthanallur in Anekal Taluk, on Bengaluru’s outskirts. His search first revealed that water was being illegally extracted from lakes in Anekal for commercial tanker supply. The extraction explained only part of their decline. Captain Santosh worked with local residents to gather evidence and secure approvals from the Minor Irrigation Department and the Deputy Commissioner of Bengaluru Urban district. Photograph: (Pinky Chandran) Between 2017 and 2019, he documented lakes and stormwater drains across the taluk. A pattern emerged. The lakes were drying because the channels that fed them had been encroached upon, built over or buried beneath concrete. For centuries, Bengaluru’s lakes had worked as an interconnected system. More than 500 years ago, under Kempe Gowda’s city planning, Raja Kaluves guided rainwater through the city’s natural valleys. Water moved from one lake to another, slowing runoff, recharging groundwater and reducing floods. As those links disappeared, rainwater began collecting on roads and in neighbourhoods. The century-old maps that revealed a lost network Captain Santosh searched historical records and found detailed British-era maps prepared in 1923. Guided by the maps, he walked through villages and neighbourhoods, comparing old waterways with today’s landscape. He traced forgotten channels and documented stretches blocked by construction and encroachment. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) While studying the link between Muthanallur Lake and Bidaraguppe Lake, he identified four historic Raja Kaluves. One had lost all visible signs of its original purpose and had become an encroached stretch of land. Captain Santosh worked with local residents to gather evidence and secure approvals from the Minor Irrigation Department and the Deputy Commissioner of Bengaluru Urban district. Together, they restored nearly four kilometres of the channel, reconnecting it to Battalakere Lake, a key link in the chain. The monsoon that put the restoration to the test The next monsoon brought proof. Neighbouring areas flooded again. Muthanallur escaped the flooding. The revived Raja Kaluve carried rainwater along its original course, directing it into interconnected lakes instead of roads and homes . Bengaluru has an estimated 800 kilometres of stormwater drains, many altered by rapid urbanisation. Photograph: (Allen Egenuse J) The result strengthened Captain Santosh’s belief that Bengaluru could recover much of its resilience by restoring the system it had inherited. He expanded the effort across Anekal Taluk, helping revive 14 ancient lakes. Many are believed to be nearly 1,000 years old, with several dating to the reign of Rajaraja Chola I. What a city can learn from its water Bengaluru has an estimated 800 kilometres of stormwater drains, many altered by rapid urbanisation. Roads and buildings have expanded across natural drainage paths, leaving rainwater with fewer routes to move safely. Speaking to The Indian Express in 2022, Captain Santosh said, “In natural settings, rainwater either gets soaked into the soil or makes its way to rain streams, lakes and rivers. If these are maintained efficiently, we will never face floods and calamities.” His work points to a simple truth: a city’s resilience can begin by remembering the pathways its water once knew. items.title: How Does a Man Go From Nearly Ending It All to Becoming the 1st Indian to Run at the North Pole?
items.blurb: By 10 on a slightly warm Kolkata morning, the city was already in full flow. Tea stalls buzzed with regulars, buses groaned through traffic, and amid that familiar bustle, Ram Gopal Kothari had carved out some time to speak with The Better India . At 44, he runs Epic Assurance Services LLP, a business he built from scratch , but even today, his life feels ruled more by discipline than comfort. When he answered the phone, there was no rush in his voice. Just a calm that comes from having lived through far more uncertainty than most people ever see. Kothari recently became the first Indian to complete a marathon at the Geographic North Pole, running 42.2 kilometres across floating ice at 90 degrees North. But when our conversation began, he was not talking about the marathon. He was talking about persistence. “I do not believe in giving up on anything I do. The moment you give up, everything ends there. But if you take one more step, something always changes,” he says. It did not sound like a line prepared for an interview. It sounded like something shaped over years, in moments when things were falling apart, and there was no audience, no reassurance, only the next step left to take. Because long before he stood on floating ice at the Geographic North Pole, he had already lived through years when even basic stability disappeared more than once. Rebuilding from zero was never a one-time effort. It became something he had to do, again and again, in different phases of his life. Burrabazar mornings, where nothing felt unusual at the time Born in 1981, he grew up in Burrabazar, Kolkata, in a modest home with an asbestos roof and shared facilities. It was a densely packed neighbourhood where daily life spilled into the streets, where children played outside because there was no space inside, and where routines were decided more by circumstance than planning. He does not recall it as a difficult childhood in the way outsiders might imagine it. For him, it was simply the world he knew. After visiting Antarctica, he began thinking about reaching the North Pole. “We never thought we were struggling; it was just normal life for us, and everyone around us lived the same way, so nothing ever felt unusual,” he tells The Better India. His father worked in a small clothing shop, earning enough to keep the household going, while his mother ensured that education was never compromised. At the centre of it all was his grandmother. “My grandmother was the emotional anchor of our family. She always taught us to be kind, to stay patient, and to believe in something bigger than whatever hardship we were facing at that moment,” he says. Those lessons found their way into everyday routines. He would wake up at 3 am to study before school, not because anyone celebrated the habit, but because it was simply what was expected. While the rest of the city was still asleep, he sat with his books, revising lessons before the day began. Among the children he grew up with, he was eventually the only one to complete graduation. At the time, it did not feel like a defining moment. It became meaningful only years later, when he looked back and realised how many small, ordinary decisions had led him there. A college experience that could have gone either way He completed his graduation from Bhawanipur Education Society College in Kolkata, where he found himself among students from very different financial backgrounds. The transition was manageable at first, but after his first year, the college increased its fees, placing unexpected pressure on his family. “My mother suggested I should consider shifting to another college,” he says. “It was becoming difficult for us at that point.” But leaving did not feel like the only option. Instead, he kept returning to the college administration, explaining his situation as honestly as he could. There was no elaborate plan, only the hope that someone would listen. “I just kept telling them I cannot manage this fee. That was all I could say,” he explains. It took several conversations over a few weeks, but the college eventually reduced his fees to an amount his family could manage, allowing him to continue his education . Looking back, it was not a dramatic turning point. There was no celebration or grand moment of relief. Yet it became one of the earliest reminders that persistence, even in the smallest of battles, could quietly change the course of his life. The first job and learning how the world actually works Soon after completing his graduation in 2002, he stepped into his first job in the home loan sector, a world that immediately felt different from anything he had known before. The role demanded higher expectations, required stringent routines, and tied outcomes directly to performance. His early assignments involved distributing pamphlets at airports and metro stations, a task that tested not just patience but also comfort levels. “I remember standing in those places thinking someone I knew might walk past,” he says. “It felt uncomfortable in the beginning, not because of the work itself, but because of perception.” However, he stayed. Till March 2008, he worked consistently, learning the basics of sales, client interaction, and the discipline required to survive in a target-driven environment. Over time, he became more stable in his role. He got married and became a father, and life briefly took on a predictable shape that felt like it might continue. On 13 July 2025, he stood at the Geographic North Pole. Then came the 2008 global financial crisis, and that stability disappeared almost overnight. When everything collapsed in layers The recession hit the financial sector hard, particularly loan-related businesses. Work slowed down, targets became harder to achieve, and eventually Ram lost his job. “There were days when I did not know how to manage even basic expenses. It felt like everything around me was uncertain,” he says. He joined HDFC Standard Life in July, trying to rebuild without delay, but that phase did not last long. Within months, he moved out and took what he describes as a difficult but necessary risk, starting a small clothing manufacturing business using a loan of four lakh rupees. By May 2009, the business had failed. Around that time, Cyclone Aila struck West Bengal, bringing incessant rain and strong winds that tore through the city. In the asbestos-roof space where he had set up his small operation, water seeped in, soaking the fabrics he had invested in and leaving them unusable. What little he had managed to build began slipping away in a matter of hours. But even beyond the damage caused by the storm, he knew the foundation itself was fragile. “The cyclone made things worse,” he says softly, “but the truth is, I was already struggling to keep the business alive.” “I had borrowed money, but there was no consistent income. Everything started collapsing together, one part after another,” he says. A phase where even survival felt uncertain A relative later helped him re-enter the general insurance industry, and for a short period, things improved. He worked long hours, rebuilt contacts, and started regaining confidence. But in May 2011, he was suddenly removed from the job. That moment became the lowest point of his life. He does not describe the following incident lightly. One day, overwhelmed by pressure and exhaustion, he went to a metro station with the intention of ending his life. There was no dramatic buildup, only a sense of having reached a point where continuing felt impossible. At that exact moment, his phone rang. It was his wife, Shipra Kothari. “I did not know where he was,” she says. “But I could sense something was wrong.” What she said was not dressed up as long reassurance, but it was enough to express her support and change his decision at that moment. “I told him we will face everything together. We will survive this,” she says. He remembers that moment as a pause that changed direction. “That call brought me back,” he adds. “It did not solve anything immediately, but it stopped what was happening inside me, and gave me a lot of hope.” After that, there was no recovery in the traditional sense. He began again from scratch. No office, no stable income, and no financial cushion. He worked from cyber cafes, preparing insurance quotations manually, and then travelled across neighbourhoods on foot to meet clients directly. “I used to walk for hours because I could not afford transport,” he says. On 22 May 2012, he formally established Epic Assurance Services LLP. It began as a small operation but celebrated the beginning of a long phase of rebuilding. “It was not big at all, but it was stable, and that mattered more than anything else,” he explains. The marathon was conducted on floating ice, in repeated loops around a marked circuit, because a continuous route is impossible in that environment. When travel began to redefine his sense of limits As the business grew, he began travelling internationally. A trip to Dubai in 2013 changed his perspective on what life could look like beyond work. Travel became less about leisure and more about exposure to extremes of geography, climate, and human experience. Over the years, he has travelled to 79 countries and seven continents, and that journey is continuing, led by a growing list of expeditions that include Antarctica, Greenland, Yakutia, and climbs such as Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Elbrus, each one adding a new layer to how he understands grit and life itself. “I started enjoying doing things I had never done before,” he says. “It kept me inquisitive.” Running enters life without planning In 2018, a conversation about the Tata Mumbai Marathon led him to take part in it, and he decided to try it for the first time. He had no formal preparation for it and no athletic background. “I was not fit at all, but I still went ahead and ran,” he says. That single event introduced him to long-distance running. After that, he continued participating in them without training or professional guidance. He explains, “I never trained like an athlete. I just kept running when I could, taking part in half marathons in Kolkata and other cities along the way. For me, it was more about learning from experience rather than formal training.” The long attempt to reach the North Pole After visiting Antarctica, he began thinking about reaching the North Pole. The idea slowly grew into participation in a marathon at 90 degrees North. He attempted it twice in 2023 and 2024, but both times the event was cancelled due to external conditions and logistical challenges. Finally, in July 2025, he travelled through Svalbard as part of an icebreaker expedition. On 13 July 2025, he stood at the Geographic North Pole. The marathon was conducted on floating ice, in repeated loops around a marked circuit, because a continuous route is impossible in that environment. The conditions were unlike anything he had experienced before, even compared to Antarctica or Greenland. The ice itself was unstable, shifting underfoot, and there was no fixed ground beneath. The race began at 8:45 am local time after a short delay caused by weather checks. The race began at 8:45 am local time after a short delay caused by weather checks. The temperature hovered around minus eight degrees Celsius, but the real challenge was not just cold; it was the combination of wind, moisture, and unstable ice layers that constantly changed under the runners’ feet. He started strongly, managing the first set of loops with controlled pace, but as the hours passed and sunlight began reflecting off the Arctic surface, the ice began to soften. Water started pooling in certain sections, turning parts of the circuit into slush. Every step required adjustment, as the surface beneath him alternated between hard ice and soft, sinking patches. “My shoes were filled with icy water, and at one point I could feel my feet going numb before sudden sharp pain set in as the cold shifted,” he says. By the 26th kilometre, conditions had changed considerably. The track near the cruise support area had become unstable, and runners were forced to carefully avoid sections where the ice was thinning. Some participants slipped, others slowed down substantially, and the overall pace dropped. He remembers that phase in detail, not as exhaustion alone, but as constant adjustment. Every loop felt slightly different from the previous one. There were moments where he had to stop briefly just to regain balance as the surface beneath him cracked or shifted unexpectedly. By the 42nd loop, exhaustion was no longer the main issue. It was pain from repeated cramps, combined with the mental strain of continuing in conditions that kept changing without warning. “I thought I might not finish, and there was a moment when stopping felt reasonable,” he admits. But he continued, moving forward with each loop, without thinking about the distance remaining. “I told myself I had already come too far to stop,” he says. He completed the marathon after 50 loops, finishing in approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes. What remains after everything With that, Ram Gopal Kothari became the first Indian to complete a marathon at the Geographic 90 degrees North Pole. But he does not describe it as a final achievement, rather as one moment in a much longer sequence of events moulded by his tendency to push through. Ram Gopal Kothari became the first Indian to complete a marathon at the Geographic 90 degrees North Pole. “When I finished, I felt I had taken India there with me,” he says. For Shipra Kothari, the journey is not defined by one day. “This is not just one achievement; it is everything he has been through and everything we have seen together,” she says. What remains is a life where stopping was always an option, but never the final decision. All pictures courtesy Ram Gopal Kothari.
